section.name: End-to-end guide: Preparing a structure for dynamics or free-energy protocols in Force Field X (FFX)
section.p: This walkthrough shows a minimal, reproducible workflow for taking a PDB ID to a production MD simulation (and is directly applicable to alchemical/free‑energy protocols once you have dual/quad topologies). It covers:

ul.li: Downloading a PDB structure
Solvating it in a periodic box (optional ions)
Energy minimization
NVT warm‑up and NPT equilibration
Production dynamics

section.p: All commands use the ffxc CLI that ships with FFX. Run any command with -h to see full options.
TIP: Put a .key file in your run directory to select the force field and common MD settings. For proteins, AMOEBA Bio 2018 is typical.
section.source:
# Choose a force field forcefield AMOEBA_BIO_2018
# Nonbonded/cutoff typical defaults are internal to FFX; override here if needed, e.g.: # a-ewald 0.545 # ewald-cutoff 7.0 # vdw-cutoff 9.0 # polarization mutual
section.p: If you don’t use a .key, many defaults still work, but being explicit is good practice for reproducibility.

subsection.name: 1) Download or prepare the starting structure
subsection.p: FFX does not impose a specific PDB downloader, so use curl/wget from the RCSB PDB (example uses ubiquitin 1UBQ):
Notes:

ul.li: Inspect and fix issues like missing residues/loops, alternate locations, non‑standard ligands, and crystallographic waters as appropriate for your study.
If you plan constant‑pH or rotamer/titration work, consult the Ph* and MutatePDB/SaveAsPDB commands.

subsection.name: 2) Solvate the structure in a periodic box (and optionally add ions)
subsection.p: Command reference: ffxc Solvator -h (see the Solvator command).
You must provide a solvent box PDB (e.g., a water box). The repo ships with examples; a safe default is:

ul.li: examples/waterbox.pdb (small equilibrated water box you can tile)

subsection.p: You can also supply an ion PDB (with a matching .ions file) to do stoichiometric ion placement.
Examples:

ul.li: Cubic box with 10 Å padding around the solute, translating solute to center:
Rectangular (non‑cubic) box with explicit lengths (Å) (skip auto padding), and place NaCl from an ion file:

subsection.p: Useful options you may tune (see Solvator -h):

ul.li: --padding <Å>: minimum solvent shell; default 9.0 Å.
--boundary <Å>: delete solvent closer than this to solute; default 2.5 Å.
--pH <value>: initialize titration states near this pH (preps for constant‑pH workflows).
--randomSeed <int>: deterministic ion placement.

subsection.p: Output: a solvated PDB adjacent to your input (e.g., 1UBQ.pdb → 1UBQ_solvated.pdb depending on your naming). The output includes periodic box info (CRYST1) so later MD knows it’s periodic.
TIP: If you prefer to keep originals untouched, copy/rename your PDB before solvating and/or direct outputs to a new directory.

subsection.name: 3) Energy minimization (relax bad contacts)
subsection.p: Command reference: ffxc Minimize -h (see the Minimize command).
Run a short L‑BFGS minimization. Start conservative on steps; increase if needed.
Notes:

ul.li: You can restrict minimization to a subset of atoms with --active selections if needed.
For alchemical systems, see the --ac/--acRes/--lambda family of options.

subsection.p: Output: an updated (lower‑energy) structure file and a log with final energies.

subsection.name: 4) NVT warm-up (gentle temperature ramp, optional)
subsection.p: Before applying pressure coupling, it’s common to stabilize temperature under constant volume. Keep time steps small at first for safety.
Example: 50 ps at 298.15 K, 1.0 fs steps, writing frames every 2.5 ps, restarts every 5 ps.
subsection.source: ffxc Dynamics \ --molecularDynamicsEngine OpenMM \ --integrator Verlet \ --thermostat Bussi \ --temperature 298.15 \ --dt 1.0 \ --numberOfSteps 50000 \ --report 0.5 \ --write 2.5 \ --checkpoint 5.0 \ --fileFormat XYZ \ 1UBQ_solvated_minimized.pdb
subsection.p: Notes:

ul.li: --fileFormat XYZ will write an .arc trajectory (compact); use PDB if you require PDB output.
--molecularDynamicsEngine OpenMM leverages GPU acceleration if available. Omit or set to FFX for CPU.
If a .dyn restart file exists next to your input, Dynamics will continue from it by default.

subsection.name: 5) NPT equilibration (apply pressure coupling and relax volume)
subsection.p: Use the Monte Carlo barostat built into Dynamics via --npt <pressure_atm>. A typical equilibration is a few hundred picoseconds to a couple nanoseconds, depending on system size.
Example: 500 ps NPT at 1 atm and 298.15 K.
subsection.source: ffxc Dynamics \ --molecularDynamicsEngine OpenMM \ --integrator Verlet \ --thermostat Bussi \ --temperature 298.15 \ --dt 1.0 \ --npt 1.0 \ --meanBarostatInterval 10 \ --isotropic \ --numberOfSteps 500000 \ --report 0.5 \ --write 2.5 \ --checkpoint 5.0 \ --fileFormat XYZ \ 1UBQ_solvated_minimized.pdb
subsection.p: Notes:

ul.li: --meanBarostatInterval sets how often barostat moves are proposed (in MD steps).
--isotropic keeps volume moves isotropic (good default for isotropic liquids).
Use --minDensity/--maxDensity bounds to reject unphysical densities during early equilibration if needed.
Keep dt=1.0 fs for AMOEBA unless you have validated larger steps for your system.

subsection.name: 6) Production MD (NPT or NVT)
subsection.p: Once density and temperature have stabilized (inspect logs), run your production trajectory. Choose NPT or NVT based on your analysis needs; many workflows keep NPT.
Example: 10 ns NPT production at 298.15 K, 1 atm.
subsection.source: ffxc Dynamics \ --molecularDynamicsEngine OpenMM \ --integrator Verlet \ --thermostat Bussi \ --temperature 298.15 \ --dt 1.0 \ --npt 1.0 \ --meanBarostatInterval 25 \ --isotropic \ --numberOfSteps 10000000 \ --report 1.0 \ --write 10.0 \ --checkpoint 10.0 \ --fileFormat XYZ \ 1UBQ_equilibrated.pdb
subsection.p: Tips:

ul.li: Adjust --report (thermo print frequency), --write (trajectory), and --checkpoint (restart) to balance file size vs. resolution.
Use different output directories per stage or rename input files to carry stage labels (*_minimized.pdb, *_equilibrated.pdb).

subsection.name: Notes for free-energy (alchemical) protocols
subsection.p: Once your structure is equilibrated and validated, you can introduce alchemical topologies and lambdas. Relevant entry points include:

ul.li: Dynamics and Minimize provide --alchemicalAtoms, --alchemicalResidues, --unchargedAtoms, and dual/quad‑topology options (--ac2, --uaA, --uaB, etc.).
Control --lambda and switching functions (--switchingFunction) during minimization/equilibration windows per lambda state.
For OSRW/expanded‑ensemble workflows, see the Examples pages and any Ph* variants for constant‑pH FE.

subsection.p: General strategy:

ol.li: Prepare/equilibrate the reference (λ=0 or λ=1) topology as above.
Introduce the alchemical masks/topologies; re‑minimize and briefly re‑equilibrate each λ before production sampling.
Ensure consistent thermostats/barostat and write intervals across λ windows for straightforward analysis.

ul.li: Force field: ensure your .key selects an appropriate AMOEBA parameter set for your system (proteins: AMOEBA_BIO_2018). Mixed systems (protein + small molecule) may require merged or custom parameter files.
Protonation/titration: for pH‑dependent studies, initialize with Solvator --pH and consider PhEnergy, PhDynamics, test.SaveAsConstantPhPDB, etc.
Ions: when using --ionFile, you must also have a co‑located .ions file with stoichiometry/valences (e.g., nacl.pdb and nacl.ions). Use --randomSeed for reproducibility.
Periodicity: solvation writes CRYST1 so MD is periodic; confirm your Dynamics logs report PME and periodic boundary conditions.
Trajectory format: XYZ (.arc) is compact for long runs; PDB is bulkier but sometimes preferred for interoperability.
Performance: prefer --molecularDynamicsEngine OpenMM on GPU; ensure GPU drivers and OpenMM are properly installed per FFX documentation.
Solvator: Prepare solvent boxes and ions around a solute.
Minimize: L‑BFGS energy minimization.
Dynamics: Time integration with thermostats/barostats.
Energy: Compute energies/gradients for spot checks.
